essential: Carter's refusal to help, and Tuppence's realization that without Tommy she is 'a rudderless ship'. Include her self-scolding about being sentimental.
No sign of Boris. Tuppence persuades a reluctant Julius ('It can do no harm') to visit Sir James on her Sunday afternoon out.
Sir James's library has one wall of works on crime. He admits his earlier remark was a hint, and he gives the 'without prejudice' young-sister warning.
Tuppence tells Sir James the whole story, including Tommy. Sir James says he has theories about Jane Finn, criticizes Carter, and decides to stay rather than go fishing.
Sir James proposes making Mrs. Vandemeyer talk, keeping bribery in reserve. Julius offers one million dollars, Sir James converts it to over £250,000, and Sir James flushes at the mention of a fee.

The plan: Tuppence returns at nine-thirty, Sir James calls at ten, and Julius waits with the car. Include Sir James's advice to have a good dinner and not think ahead. Keep Tuppence's 'Isn't he a duck?' and Julius's grudging concession.

Tuppence walks in the park, then is drawn back to South Audley Mansions. Albert reports that Rita is packing and has sent for a taxi. Tuppence sends him to telephone Julius, or failing that Sir James.
Tuppence's toothache excuse; the cook has been sent out; the revolver at her temple; the disordered, half-packed bedroom.
Rita demands she drink the sleeping draught. Include the 'poison?'/'Perhaps' exchange and Rita's argument that she does not want a murder hue and cry.
Tuppence stages a grovelling collapse to gain time and get closer. She extracts the oath, throws the glass in Rita's face, and seizes the revolver. Include Rita's 'I have a long memory' threat.

The bribe: Tuppence recalls Boris's 'sell--us' remark and Whittington's 'Rita?'. She offers £100,000 (not the whole million) from an American millionaire friend. Rita can find out where Jane is and will ask Boris about Tommy.

'Who is Mr. Brown?': Rita pales, admits she knows ('I was beautiful... Not beautiful enough'), and demands an oath of secrecy and the money without delay. She then fears listeners ('walls might have ears'), shrieks, points over Tuppence's head, and faints.

voice_profile: Brisk, comic thriller narration in third person, staying mostly close to Tuppence's mind. Her self-mockery ('Little fool') and her money creed are played for comedy but also expose real feeling. The prose is mostly fast dialogue in distinct voices: Julius's American slang ('Sure thing', 'Put me wise', 'Bully'); Sir James's dry, smooth legal phrasing and chin-stroking; Mrs. Vandemeyer's steely melodrama; Albert's cinema-fed Cockney. Short narrative paragraphs carry the sudden reversals. Chapters end on hooks such as 'Now-- _it was empty_.' Emphasis is marked with italics. Double hyphens and broken-off speeches ('----') convey interruption and dread.

essential: Rita revives, says she mustn't talk ('It's my heart'), and Sir James pronounces 'She'll do now.'
Anticlimax. Julius is sure the money will look as good in the morning. Sir James wishes they had not interrupted when they did.
They decide not to leave the flat. Tuppence notes Rita's fear of Brown and the walls having ears; Julius suggests a dictaphone. Sir James insists they stay 'for Mrs. Vandemeyer's sake'.

Tuppence glimpses fear and malevolence on Rita's half-open face and wonders whether the faint was a sham. Rita then whispers 'Don't--leave', 'sleepy', 'Mr.--Brown'. Tuppence promises to sit up all night.
Tuppence searches the wardrobe and under the bed and finds nothing. Sir James has her lock the door from outside and take the key.
Julius explains how they got in: Albert's call, the coal lift, the scullery. He goes down to reassure Albert. They keep watch in the boudoir, and Tuppence refuses to go to bed.
Night fears and Tuppence's 'I feel he's here'. Sir James says it is not humanly possible for anyone to be in the flat. Then dawn breaks, and Tuppence wants to be made a Dame.
Tea with a fourth cup for 'the prisoner'. Tuppence fears Rita may have escaped, and Sir James says nothing. Rita is found dead, apparently in her sleep, some hours earlier.
'If it is luck.' Sir James rules out entry and says 'We must find out'. The open window and the balcony are dismissed. The charred papers in the grate; the safe; Julius's pause before 'Nothing'.
The doctor says heart failure or a sleeping-draught overdose and smells chloral. Tuppence checks the bottle and finds it empty.

essential: Sir James smoothly arranges matters. The doctor accepts an accidental chloral overdose and doubts an inquest will be needed; a nurse arrives.
Julius despairs. Sir James proposes Dr. Hall at the Métropole after bath and breakfast.
Hall greets Julius as the 'tree episode' man.

Sir James asks his questions in private. He hesitates before confirming that the matter concerns testimony. He calls the girl's name immaterial because it will be assumed, and asks whether Hall knows Mrs. Vandemeyer.
Hall learns of the death; 'Accidentally, it is believed. I should not like to say myself'; Sir James found her dead.
Mrs. Vandemeyer committed her 'niece' Janet Vandemeyer to Hall in June or July 1915. The girl was said to have been on the Lusitania with her. She is sane.
Total loss of memory before 7 May 1915. Her first memory is landing with the survivors; she did not know her name and could not speak her own tongue. Keep Hall's ghoulish interest in the case.
Hall suggested a Paris specialist, but Mrs. Vandemeyer opposed publicity, and Sir James remarks grimly that he can imagine it. Memory will return suddenly, and she will forget the period in between.

Julius's staged-shipwreck plan: hire a liner, passengers and a submarine, with artistes screaming; 'graft'. Hall is aghast and protests the expense. Sir James confirms Julius's wealth, and Hall becomes deferential.
Julius asks for Jane to be brought; the closing reveal.

essential: Janet left last Wednesday, the night of Julius's fall, after an urgent message from Mrs. Vandemeyer. She left with her nurse on the night train. Julius remembers 'Nurse Edith--left with a patient'.
Sir James warns Tuppence silent with a glance. He tells Hall not to go to the police, saying the girl is probably with relations.
Outside, Sir James suggests advertising for the nurse but holds out little hope. He shakes his head at Julius over Tuppence's head and announces he is leaving for Scotland.
His low-voiced hint to Tuppence: holiday-time isn't all playtime, and 'Never tell all you know'.
Tuppence recalls Julius's pause at the safe and withholds the hint from him ('Nothing particular').
Drive in the park. Julius is discouraged, dislikes Sir James but thinks he would not quit if there were a chance, and talks of going back to the States. Tuppence insists they must find Tommy.
Julius asks about Tuppence and Beresford, and she says 'friends--nothing more'. She restates that she will marry money.
Julius proposes with businesslike frankness and is refused. Keep 'Because of Beresford?' / 'No, no, _no!_'. He asks her to think it over until tomorrow.
At the mirror she scolds herself, sobs over Tommy's snapshot, and admits she loves him, making it a matter of principles betrayed.
She wonders about the safe, reviews last night against Sir James's words, and is struck by an 'impossible' idea. Do not specify it.
She writes a carefully worded note to Julius, leaves it in his empty room, and receives a telegram she believes is from Tommy.
